stops.name: Olta, the head of the Chacho
stops.campa: Governor of his own province and director of the war against the montonera of La Rioja, he presides over the pursuit of Ángel Vicente Peñaloza, the Chacho, who is run down at Olta, killed with a lance, and beheaded, his head set on a pike in the plaza of San Juan Bautista de Olta. Two years earlier Sarmiento had written to Mitre the sentence that will follow him forever: do not try to economise gaucho blood. The book that read the caudillo as a desert chieftain has become a government that treats him as one.
stops.quote: No trate de economizar sangre de gauchos. Este es un abono que es preciso hacer útil al país.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Sarmiento a Bartolomé Mitre, Buenos Aires, 20 de septiembre de 1861

stops.name: New York, the legation and the loss of Dominguito
stops.campa: Minister plenipotentiary to the United States, he spends three years measuring a republic in mid-reconstruction, receives an honorary doctorate at Ann Arbor, corresponds with Mary Mann, who is translating Facundo into English, and is elected president of Argentina without campaigning, from abroad. In the middle of it comes the telegram: his adopted son Domingo Fidel, twenty-one, has fallen in the assault at Curupaytí in Paraguay. He writes the boy's life as a book. The war he will inherit has already taken the only son he had.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the oath of office
stops.campa: He comes ashore from the legation and is sworn in as president of a country he has spent most of his adult life outside of. The programme was written in 1849 and has not changed: schools, immigrants, railways, telegraph, statistics, an observatory, a navy. He inherits a war in Paraguay he did not want, a rebellion in Entre Ríos, and a treasury with nothing in it. The schoolmaster of Pocuro, who once earned thirteen pesos a month, now has a state to build the schoolhouse with.

stops.name: Paraná, the Escuela Normal and the teachers from the north
stops.campa: He signs the decree founding the first national normal school of Argentina at Paraná, which will open its doors the August after next; and to staff the system he sends for teachers from the United States: sixty-five women and a handful of men, recruited largely through Mary Mann, who cross an ocean to Entre Ríos, Tucumán, Catamarca, San Juan, learning Spanish as they go. Some die of fever, most stay for life. It is the largest deliberate import of pedagogy in the hemisphere's history, and it is the Massachusetts common school, and behind that the Swiss method, arriving in the Río de la Plata.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the yellow fever
stops.campa: Yellow fever takes some fourteen thousand people out of a city of under two hundred thousand; the government dissolves, the rich abandon San Telmo forever and move north, and carts collect the dead. Sarmiento is criticised for leaving the capital and never lives it down. Out of the catastrophe come the things he actually believed in: a new cemetery at Chacarita, and the beginning of the water and drainage works that end the epidemic era. The statistician's republic is founded on a plague pit.

stops.name: Córdoba, the Observatorio Astronómico
stops.campa: He brings Benjamin Gould from Cambridge to build an observatory in Córdoba and Germán Burmeister to found an academy of sciences beside it, and he inaugurates the dome himself. From it will come the Uranometría Argentina and the Córdoba Durchmusterung, the first systematic mapping of the southern sky, catalogued from a provincial city of the interior. The man who read the pampa as a desert of ignorance answers it, finally, by pointing an instrument at the part of heaven Europe cannot see.

stops.name: Paraná, the first jardín de infantes
stops.campa: Thirty-five children between three and six are enrolled in the kindergarten annexed to the normal school at Paraná, organised and directed by Sara Chamberlain de Eccleston, one of the North American teachers he brought over. She founds the Argentine Froebelian Society and translates the manuals of the Gifts. The idea reached Sarmiento through Mary Mann and the Peabody sisters; it reaches Entre Ríos through a widow from Philadelphia. Froebel comes to the Plata by way of Boston, forty years after Blankenburg, and the old man is alive to see it.

stops.name: Asunción, the death on the river
stops.campa: Old, deaf, asthmatic and out of office, he goes up the river to Asunción for the warmth and stays to work: schools, a newspaper, contracts for more teachers, eucalyptus and willow planted in the Paraguayan heat. He dies there of heart failure on the eleventh of September, seventy-seven years old, in the capital of the country his own government helped destroy, on the far side of a river, in exile one last time by choice. The state that carried him home is the state he built.

stops.name: Recoleta, the return of the body
stops.campa: The body comes down the Paraná by steamer, met at every port by schoolchildren, and is buried in the Recoleta ten days after the death. Carlos Pellegrini speaks the sentence the country has kept: that this was the most powerful brain America has produced. The eleventh of September becomes the Day of the Teacher across the hemisphere. He wanted no monument but a school, and got both: an obelisk of a tomb, and by the last count of his life more than a thousand eight hundred schoolhouses.
